paras: The hanging of three horse thieves in Hill County, Texas, was the reported killing, shortly before April 8, 1881, of three unnamed men accused of horse theft by "vigilantes of Johnson county" who overtook them in neighboring Hill County. The story circulated only as a one-line wire item, and no report named the men, gave their race, or described the hanging.

According to the Austin Weekly Democratic Statesman, the three had "been operating in Johnson county" before they were "lately captured in Hill county and hanged." No report described the thefts they were accused of or any complaint, warrant, or arrest.

The earliest dispatch, dated Galveston, April 8, relayed a Dallas report to the News that the three "were overtaken in Hill county by vigilantes of Johnson county and summarily disposed of." Other versions said plainly that they were "hanged" or "lynched." None gave the date, the place of the hanging, the number of vigilantes, or whether anyone watched.
No report of an inquest, arrests, or any official response appears in the coverage.

The item reached papers far from Texas within days: the Memphis Public Ledger ran it on April 9 among "Morning Telegrams in Brief," and a paper titled The Daily Gazette printed it on April 11 under the headline "THREE MEN HANGED BY VIGILANTES." The Hopkinsville South Kentuckian listed it on April 12 under "General News," and the Richmond (Mo.) Democrat placed it on April 14 among "Crimes and Casualties." Weekly news summaries in Iowa and Michigan repeated the phrase "summarily disposed of," set in quotation marks, in their columns of Southern news.

The only Texas paper in the coverage, the Austin Statesman, ran it on April 21 between an item on sheep flocks and one on Major Penn's plan to save "the sinners of Harrisville, Bell county", without comment. No paper editorialized, and none mentioned race.

The Memphis brief placed the hanging "in Johnson county," while the fuller dispatch and the Austin paper said the men were taken in Hill County by Johnson County vigilantes. Separately, the Dallas Daily Herald reported on April 10 that "the report that two horse thieves were lynched near morgan in the Brazos. bottoms" was "a canard." That item gave a different number and place and did not mention Hill or Johnson county, so the coverage does not show whether it addressed the same report.

bases: Three men described as horse thieves were reported hanged by Johnson County 'vigilantes' after being overtaken in Hill County, and one paper called it a lynching (A3, A5, A9).

The papers report three alleged horse thieves hanged by 'vigilantes' with no legal process and call it a lynching (A1, A3, A5, A9); the vigilantes' number is not given, though the term implies a group (A3, A6).

Every report is a brief that appears to descend from one Dallas dispatch relayed through Galveston on April 8 (A3); the variants (A1, A5, A9) add no independent detail, and a Dallas paper's denial of a different-sounding lynching report (A2) neither confirms nor clearly contradicts it.

framing.detail: Out-of-state papers ran the item as a one-line brief among other crime and general news, using the euphemism 'summarily disposed of' (A3, A6) or plain 'hanged' (A1) and 'lynched' (A5).
The Austin Statesman listed it without comment among miscellaneous 'Texas Facts and Fancies' (A9).

conflicts.note: The fuller Galveston-relayed dispatch (A3) and the Texas paper (A9) say the thieves were taken in Hill County by Johnson County vigilantes; the Memphis brief (A1) appears to have compressed this to Johnson County.
